stances.claim: The country needs modern airports, expressways, railways, water systems, electric power, and other infrastructures, but the government lacks the funds to build and skill to operate them -- the solution is public-private partnerships (PPP) mainly via the build-operate-transfer (BOT) system, where private concessionaires construct at sole expense, no public funds are spent, government earns and acquires the projects free of charge after the agreed 25-year concession. Concessionaires recoup investments plus reasonable profit from user fees, with periodic adjustments by regulatory agencies under pre-agreed rate-setting formulas.

Failed PPP: NAIA 3 -- after 20 years of disputes, still unfinished; government has 'spent at least P2 billion' in litigation/arbitration fees (Jan 6 2011 Inquirer editorial), will spend another P1.9 billion to complete by next year, and per the Aug 7 CA decision will have to pay $371 million as just compensation to Piatco. Moreover, NAIA 3 has become a drag on tourism because it cannot serve the additional millions lured by the 'It's more fun in the Philippines' campaign.

Successful PPP: Manila Water Company (eastern Metro Manila; Maynilad serves the western half) -- widely hailed as a model PPP by the IMF and World Bank; fully funded by private investors; has paid royalties since 1997; reduced water leakage from 67% to 11% (saving 700M cubic meters daily, equivalent to a P25-billion dam); grown from 3M customers (only 26% with 24/7 supply) to 6.3M customers (all 24/7, with 1.7M poor at subsidized rates); invested P75 billion in capital expenditures. Recently attacked for allegedly profiting unreasonably and charging taxes to consumers -- Manila Water replied it had faithfully observed 'the agreement that was written, reviewed, approved and guaranteed by the Philippine government.'

Timid PPP: the P60-billion Light Rail Extension to Cavite -- only one pre-qualified bidder filed a 'conditional' bid; the others backed out due to 'unattractive and unbankable' terms. Fares were fixed at a very low rate; no realistic fare-adjustment mechanism was allowed (preventing equipment-replacement, maintenance, satisfactory service, reasonable profit); concessionaires were required to shoulder real estate taxes (initially about P2 billion a year, escalating) on land they would not own. Why should they pay these taxes?

Investors have choices on what projects to invest in and in what country. Simple alternatives illustrate: in 1988 Forbes Park lots sold at P5,000/sqm; 25 years (the normal PPP concession period) later, the same lots sell at P200,000/sqm (40x more); Ayala Alabang P1,000 → P45,000/sqm (45x more); Jollibee shares P10 → P162 (16x more, not counting cash dividends). It seems that the failed NAIA 3 and the belated criticisms of the successful Manila Water PPP have resulted in over-cautiousness to the point of timidity in the Cavite LRT bidding.

While every effort must be made to avoid the lapses of NAIA 3 and to secure the best terms possible for the public, no PPP project will be undertaken if the bidding terms are not viable and concessionaires are not allowed reasonable returns. When PPP investors deliver and build infrastructures the government cannot provide and operate, they should be commended, not unfairly deprived of contracted returns on their long-term investments. The least government should do is to honor sovereign commitments and observe the sanctity of contracts -- only then will it truly inspire inclusive growth that creates jobs, alleviates poverty, and promotes prosperity.

notable_anecdotes: The three-PPP-contrast taxonomy (Failed/Successful/Timid) -- among CJP's tightest tripartite frameworks, with NAIA 3 / Manila Water / Cavite LRT each carrying its own statistical anchor.

Manila Water statistics -- 67%-to-11% leakage reduction saving 700M cubic meters daily (= P25-billion dam equivalent), 3M → 6.3M customers with 1.7M poor subsidized, P75B capex -- among the most concentrated PPP-success-statistics catalogs in the corpus.
The Cavite LRT 'unattractive and unbankable' quote -- from the failed-bidders explanation, sharp diagnostic shorthand for what was wrong with the auction terms.

The 'private investors will not own the land on which the rails shall be built. Why then should they pay these taxes?' rhetorical-question -- a clean structural-fairness critique anchored in property-rights logic.

The investor-alternatives arithmetic -- Forbes Park (40x), Ayala Alabang (45x), Jollibee (16x) -- using 1988-to-2013 25-year comparisons matched to PPP concession period as a real-options vivid contrast.

Manila Water's reply quotation about 'the agreement that was written, reviewed, approved and guaranteed by the Philippine government' -- concise pacta-sunt-servanda defense against retroactive critics, captured verbatim.

The closing 'inclusive growth that creates jobs, alleviate poverty and promote prosperity' -- CJP's FLP-aligned closing register, tying private-sector partnership to the Liberty-and-Prosperity philosophical project.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the public-private-partnership (PPP) build-operate-transfer (BOT) system through three contrasting Philippine examples. The framework: the country needs modern airports, expressways, railways, water systems, electric power, and other infrastructures, but the government lacks both the funds to build them and the skill to operate them. Under BOT, private concessionaires construct at sole expense (no public funds spent); the government earns without spending and acquires the projects free after 25 years; concessionaires recoup investments plus reasonable profit from user fees adjusted periodically by regulatory agencies under pre-agreed formulas. Failed PPP: NAIA Terminal 3 -- after 20 years of disputes, still unfinished; the government has spent at least P2 billion in litigation/arbitration fees (Jan 6 2011 Inquirer editorial), will spend another P1.9 billion to complete next year, and per the Aug 7 CA decision will have to pay $371 million as just compensation to Piatco; NAIA 3 has become a drag on tourism, unable to serve the millions lured by 'It's more fun in the Philippines.' Successful PPP: Manila Water Company (the eastern half of Metro Manila; the western half is supplied by Maynilad) -- widely hailed as a model PPP by the IMF and World Bank; fully funded by private investors; has religiously paid royalties since 1997; reduced water leakage from 67% to 11% (saving 700 million cubic meters daily -- equivalent to a P25-billion dam); grown from 3 million customers (only 26% with 24/7 supply) to 6.3 million customers (all 24/7, with 1.7 million poor at subsidized rates); invested P75 billion in capital expenditures for potable surging water. Recently attacked for allegedly profiting unreasonably and charging taxes to consumers, Manila Water replied it had faithfully observed 'the agreement that was written, reviewed, approved and guaranteed by the Philippine government.' Probably still pondering the lessons of these two contrasting programs, the present government has been slow on new PPPs -- only two projects bid out in three years (the P2-billion Daang Hari-South Luzon Expressway link and the P15-billion NAIA toll road). Timid PPP: the P60-billion Light Rail Extension to Cavite -- only one pre-qualified bidder filed a 'conditional' bid; the others backed out due to 'unattractive and unbankable' terms. Fares were fixed too low; no realistic fare-adjustment mechanism was allowed (preventing equipment-replacement, proper maintenance, satisfactory service, reasonable profit); the government wanted concessionaires to shoulder real estate taxes (initially about P2 billion a year, escalating) on land they would not own -- why should they pay these taxes? Investors have choices on what projects to invest in and in what country. Consider: in 1988 Forbes Park lots sold at P5,000/sqm; 25 years (the normal PPP concession period) later, P200,000/sqm (40x); Ayala Alabang P1,000 → P45,000/sqm (45x); Jollibee shares P10 → P162 (16x, not counting dividends). It seems the failed NAIA 3 and the belated criticisms of the successful Manila Water PPP have produced over-cautiousness to the point of timidity in the Cavite LRT bidding. While every effort must be made to avoid the NAIA 3 lapses and to secure the best terms for the public, no PPP project will be undertaken if bidding terms are not viable and concessionaires are not allowed reasonable returns. When PPP investors deliver on their contracts and build infrastructures the government cannot provide, they should be commended, not unfairly deprived of contracted returns. The least government should do is honor sovereign commitments and observe the sanctity of contracts -- only then will it truly inspire inclusive growth that creates jobs, alleviates poverty, and promotes prosperity.
